horizon.elevation.title: Terrain horizon elevation
horizon.elevation.definition: For each azimuth and observer height: the largest elevation angle, above the plane perpendicular to the radial direction at the site, of the straight line from the observer to any terrain point along the great circle of that azimuth, out to the search radius. Negative when the terrain horizon lies below the horizontal.
horizon.elevation.algorithm: Great-circle rays on a sphere. Exact triangle observer - terrain point - centre of the Moon, tan(e) = (r_t cos g - r_o) / (r_t sin g), evaluated in a cancellation-free form; curvature is contained in the formula. Each ray is covered by a lattice of points half a pixel apart. Near the site every lattice point is evaluated on the finest data. Farther out the lattice is grouped into cells; a cell is skipped only if the block maximum of the terrain over the cell proves that nothing in it can reach the horizon already found, otherwise it is walked point by point on the finest data. Crossings of the ray with the lines through pixel centres (the creases of the bilinear surface) are evaluated as well, and the leading points are refined by nested sampling. All observer heights share the same terrain evaluations.
horizon.elevation.frame: local East/North/Up at the site; up is the outward radial direction of the reference sphere

parameters.interpolation: bilinear between pixel centres, finest product that covers the point

limits: The terrain is the bilinear surface through the DEM pixels: relief smaller than a pixel is absent, and a crest between pixels is cut. Within about 1 km of the site this, not the algorithm, limits the accuracy.

horizon.far_field_bound.title: Bound on unseen far terrain
horizon.far_field_bound.definition: far_field_max_deg: the largest amount, over all azimuths and observer heights, by which terrain beyond the reach of the rays could still raise the horizon, if no such terrain is higher than ceiling_height_m. 0 means the search radius is proven sufficient under that assumption. far_field_open_azimuth_fraction: share of azimuths with a non-zero bound. shortest_reach_m: shortest ray reach (search radius, or the edge of the data).
horizon.far_field_bound.algorithm: A point of height H at central angle g from an observer at radius r_o is seen at elevation atan2((R+H) cos g - r_o, (R+H) sin g), which grows with H and, beyond the tangent point, falls with g. The bound is that elevation for H = ceiling at the end of each ray, minus the horizon found, floored at zero.
horizon.far_field_bound.frame: local East/North/Up at the site; up is the outward radial direction of the reference sphere

timeline.direction.title: Direction and apparent size of the body
timeline.direction.definition: Azimuth and elevation of the centre of the disc and its angular radius, seen from the ground point of the site. Elevation is measured from the local horizontal plane, not from the visible horizon.
timeline.direction.algorithm: Direction-table vectors interpolated to the sample time (4-point Lagrange), minus the site position vector, projected on East, North, Up; angular radius = asin(body radius / distance).
timeline.direction.frame: local East/North/Up of the site; Up is the normal of the reference sphere; azimuth clockwise from north

evidence: Test validation/tests/test_horizons.py (comparison with JPL Horizons, thresholds fixed beforehand in validation/horizons/thresholds.json).

28 Horizons cases, 95676 rows: largest direction difference 0.099 arcsec through this table, 0.005 arcsec with the observer at the site (threshold 1 arcsec). Report: validation/horizons/results/validation_table.md.

limits: Stored as 32-bit floats: azimuth resolution about 0.1 arcsec.
Observer height above the ground is not applied to the direction (below 0.01 arcsec for heights of metres).

timeline.events.title: Rise and set events
timeline.events.definition: Instants at which the visibility condition of the body (the 'threshold' of the event) starts or stops holding. 'visible_fraction > 0' means the first or last part of the disc (upper limb); 'margin_deg > 0' means the centre of the disc.
timeline.events.algorithm: The governing signal (upper-limb margin, centre margin, lower-limb margin or visible fraction) is sampled every 60 s; every change of sign is located by bisection until the bracket is at most 0.5 s wide; the middle of the bracket is reported. The closing rate is the change of the governing margin over +/-30 s. The horizon is the terrain horizon profile of this package, linearly interpolated in azimuth.
timeline.events.frame: local East/North/Up of the site; Up is the normal of the reference sphere; azimuth clockwise from north

evidence: core/tests/events/test_events.py: analytic cases (linear motion, diurnal arc, terrain ramp, short occultation, grazing pass) within 1 s.
core/tests/events/test_site_timeline.py::test_sun_events_match_direct_spice_crossings: smooth-sphere events within 1 s of direct SPICE.

limits: Numerical accuracy 0.25 s for the given inputs; two crossings closer together than 60 s can be missed.
The accuracy of event times is set by the terrain horizon, not by the ephemeris: near the poles a horizon error of 0.01 deg can move an event by many minutes.
No published sunrise or sunset clock time of a real lander was found to compare with; the operational records of two landers bound the computed events from one side only (validation/landers).

timeline.station_links.title: Direct-to-Earth windows per ground station and relay need
timeline.station_links.definition: A two-way link with a station is geometrically possible when the station (a point on the Earth) is above the terrain horizon of the site and the site is at least 10 deg above the station's horizon; 'receive' uses 6 deg. The network window is the union over the three Deep Space Network complexes, each represented by its 70 m antenna. Relay need: 0 direct link possible at all times; 1 interrupted only by station gaps; 2 interrupted by lunar terrain for part of the time; 3 no station ever above the lunar terrain.
timeline.station_links.algorithm: Station positions and local verticals relative to the Moon's centre, tabulated every 600 s in the Moon body-fixed frame (SPICE, LT+S) and interpolated; both conditions sampled every 120 s; changes located by bisection to 0.5 s. The horizon is the terrain horizon profile of this package, linearly interpolated in azimuth.
timeline.station_links.frame: local East/North/Up of the site; Up is the normal of the reference sphere; azimuth clockwise from north

parameters.mask_source: DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook 810-005, module 301 'Coverage and Geometry', Rev. N, 15 April 2022

evidence: core/tests/events/test_stations.py: window logic on cases with a known answer; fast path against direct SPICE.

validation/stations: both ends of the link against JPL Horizons, 12 queries, 3468 rows: lunar site seen from the station within 0.42 arcsec, station seen from the lunar site within 0.21 arcsec (threshold 1 arcsec). The windows themselves have not been compared with an external source.

limits: Geometry only: no link budget, antenna pattern, frequency, weather or station scheduling.
Station masks are single elevation limits; the azimuth-dependent horizon masks of the stations, the 13.5 deg limit for high-power transmit and the keyhole near the zenith are not modelled.
Only the three Deep Space Network complexes; other networks would shorten the station gaps but cannot remove an outage caused by lunar terrain.
Near the lunar horizon a real link suffers from multipath; the lunar-end mask is 0 deg here.
The accuracy of event times is set by the terrain horizon, not by the ephemeris: near the poles a horizon error of 0.01 deg can move an event by many minutes.

timeline.visible_fraction.title: Visible fraction of the disc
timeline.visible_fraction.definition: Fraction of the area of the disc that is above the horizon, 0 to 1. The disc is uniform (no limb darkening).
timeline.visible_fraction.algorithm: The disc is cut into 63 vertical strips (Gauss-Chebyshev nodes of the second kind); in each strip the part above the horizon at the strip's azimuth is taken exactly; the strips are summed with their area weights. The horizon is the terrain horizon profile of this package, linearly interpolated in azimuth.
timeline.visible_fraction.frame: local East/North/Up of the site; Up is the normal of the reference sphere; azimuth clockwise from north

evidence: core/tests/events/test_events.py::test_visible_fraction_matches_closed_form_on_flat_horizon: within 0.002 of the closed form for a straight horizon (measured 0.00006).

limits: The accuracy of event times is set by the terrain horizon, not by the ephemeris: near the poles a horizon error of 0.01 deg can move an event by many minutes.
The horizon profile must be sampled finer than the disc radius (0.26 deg for the Sun) for the fraction to be meaningful.
This fraction is cut by the terrain only. Eclipses of the Sun by the Earth are given as the windows 'sun_eclipsed_by_earth' and 'sun_totally_eclipsed_by_earth'.

timeline.windows.title: Visibility windows
timeline.windows.definition: Intervals during which the stated condition holds. '*_visible' uses the scenario threshold; '*_any_part_visible' and '*_full_disc_visible' bracket the partial phase: between them the disc is partly hidden and 'visible_fraction' says how much. 'sun_eclipsed_by_earth' and 'sun_totally_eclipsed_by_earth' are eclipses of the Sun by the Earth seen from the site; 'sun_lit' is 'sun_any_part_visible' without the total eclipses.
timeline.windows.algorithm: Built from the refined event times; 'sun_and_earth_visible' is the intersection of the two '*_visible' sets. Eclipse contacts: the separation of the Sun and the Earth seen from the site equals the sum (partial) or the difference (total) of their angular radii; Earth as an opaque disc of its equatorial radius without atmosphere; located by bisection like the events. A window that touches the start or the end of the computed range is marked clipped.
timeline.windows.frame: local East/North/Up of the site; Up is the normal of the reference sphere; azimuth clockwise from north

evidence: core/tests/events/test_events.py::test_windows_and_countdown; core/tests/test_timeline.py (interval arithmetic).

validation/pgda: the long-term share of time with any part of the Sun, and of the Earth, above the terrain horizon agrees with the published LOLA illumination maps at 100 points on terrain of the same 60 m resolution (median absolute difference 0.0006 and 0.0004; permanent shadow agrees at all 98 points compared). This checks long-term shares, not individual window edges.

validation/lro_images: sunlit or shadowed state against two dated LROC images. The shadowed state of the south pole on 18 May 2022 agrees. Along an image strip of 13 December 2010 the agreement is 89.3 % of 298 points against a registered criterion of 90 %: a failed check, in which every disagreement is ground this method calls sunlit at grazing incidence and the image rule reads as shadow.

Eclipse contacts: core/tests/events/test_eclipse.py (analytic pass within 1 s) and validation/eclipse (eclipse of 14 March 2025 at a lander site: within 0.9 min of the operator's predicted contacts, inside NASA's whole-Moon contacts).

limits: The accuracy of event times is set by the terrain horizon, not by the ephemeris: near the poles a horizon error of 0.01 deg can move an event by many minutes.
Eclipses: the Earth's atmosphere is not modelled; the real edge of the shadow is soft over about a minute and totality is dim, not black.
